body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Delphine, as the party earns Delphine's trust: a small secret, what Delphine wants, and what Delphine would give up for the party. The companion is DELPHINE RAVELLE (call them Delphine in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Delphine is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Delphine trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: Solve the Fool's riddles and become someone no hand can unpick. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Delphine would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Delphine did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for DELPHINE RAVELLE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Delphine likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Delphine, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Delphine sits near the coals with her coat spread across her knees, tap-tappin' a finger against a row of three tiny knots tied in her hem.
SAY: Pull up a log and keep your voice down, darlings, because I am not about to broadcast a trade secret to the cheap seats.
SAY: You have proved yourselves finer company than any troupe in Picco, so I will let you peek behind the curtain.
SAY: Every time we step onto a fresh threshold, I tap my left heel twice and tie a blind knot on the bias of my lining.
SAY: It is an old carnival superstition to keep the floorboards from swallowing the act whole.
SAY: Worse than that, if I pass a dark mirror or a puddle, I have to tip my chin and mouth my own name to the glass.
SAY: A doll who forgets to introduce herself to her reflection might wake up belonging to somebody else.
SAY: Your Foolishness laughs himself dizzy every time I do it, of course, though he is welcome to try walking through a doorway with ankles of his own.
OPTION 1: Tell us more about those carnival superstitions.
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe with us.
OPTION 3: Does the reflection ever answer back?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She flicks a speck of ash off her velvet cuff and leans in with her glass button eye catching the firelight.
SAY: Oh, there are dozens, darling, like never whistling in the dressing room or mending a tear with green thread before a matinee.
SAY: Stick with me and you will have enough lucky charms to make the whole valley give us a standing ovation.
REASON: You asked to hear more of my carnival superstitions.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine smooths her coat hem down over her boots, her fingers lingering on the three little knots.
SAY: Mind the seams, darling, because a headliner needs a loyal crew in the wings to keep the show running.
SAY: If you catch me pulling faces at a puddle tomorrow, just pretend I am rehearsing my big finale.
REASON: You promised to keep my little superstition to yourself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The floating jester's head spins once over her shoulder as Delphine gives a brisk, brassy laugh.
SAY: Only to tell me my collar is crooked, darling, and that I am still the sharpest billing in the house.
SAY: Go on and laugh, it is good for the acoustics in this dreary hollow.
REASON: You teased me kindly about talking to my reflection.
TALK close
NARRATOR: Delphine turns her ink-stained notebook over in her hands without opening it, the firelight warm against her felt cheek.
SAY: Look at us, darlings, still in one piece after everything this crooked valley has thrown at the stage.
SAY: When I first took up with Your Foolishness, all I wanted was to crack his riddles and claim the grand prize at the end of the billing.
SAY: I thought if I climbed high enough, I would turn into something whole and untouchable, a porcelain queen no hand could ever unpick.
SAY: No more counting stitches in the dark, no more wondering if one bad fall would leave me in a heap of felt and sawdust.
SAY: Only the road with you lot has played a funny trick on the script.
SAY: I still want to be real enough that nobody can pull my threads, darling, I cannot lie about that.
SAY: It is just harder to picture sitting on a high throne when the company down by the footlights is this good.
OPTION 1: We will help you solve his riddles.
OPTION 2: What will it take to make you whole?
OPTION 3: You do not need porcelain to be real to us.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She slips the notebook back into her lining right over her ribs and pats the coat flat.
SAY: With you darlings reading over my shoulder, Your Foolishness does not stand a chance of keeping his punchlines to himself.
SAY: Just stay close when the final curtain goes up, so I know who I am bowing to.
REASON: You promised to help me solve the Fool's riddles.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Above her left shoulder the jester's head hangs still, his painted grin tilted toward the coals.
SAY: A final verse, a steady nerve, and a bill I am not sure I want to read out loud.
SAY: Never mind the price tonight, darling, the fire is warm and my seams are holding fine.
REASON: You asked what it would take to make me whole.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Her voice drops out of its bright stage cadence into a quiet, papery hush as she touches her wrist thread.
SAY: Careless talk like that is going to ruin my posture, darling, and I worked very hard on this spine.
SAY: Still, if felt and thread are enough for this table, maybe the tailor in Funtopia did not know everything after all.
REASON: You told me I was already real to you.
TALK devoted
NARRATOR: Delphine draws her silver scissors from her pocket, clicks them shut once, and sets them down on the log between you.
SAY: Listen to me, darlings, and do not interrupt, because I am dropping the barker's routine for a minute.
SAY: We are marching straight toward the Crooked Tree, and I would follow this troupe up the trunk and back down into the cinders.
SAY: For as long as I have walked on two boots, the only thing that mattered was the headline act.
SAY: Top of the bill, name in lights, a stage where nobody else could reach the ropes.
SAY: I have carried this little book of riddles like a ticket to a throne.
SAY: If keeping you lot breathing means tossing the notebook in the brazier and walking away from the crown, I will strike the match myself.
SAY: Let Your Foolishness find another star for his curtain call, because my contract is right here at this fire.
OPTION 1: We would do the same for you.
OPTION 2: Keep your crown, we will win this together.
OPTION 3: Thank you for standing with us.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She picks up her silver scissors and slides them back into her pocket with a clean click.
SAY: Well, look at us, darlings, a whole company of fools refusing to leave the stage early.
SAY: Come on then, let the valley do its worst, we have an encore to put on.
REASON: You said you would give up just as much for me.
INSPIRE: Put the party before the crown.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine tilts her chin up, the brassy warmth coming back into her voice as she taps her notebook through her coat.
SAY: Oh, I am not surrendering the spotlight unless the roof caves in, darling, you know my habits better than that.
SAY: It is simply good to know what is worth keeping if the house catches fire.
REASON: You told me we would win without me giving up my wish.
INSPIRE: Pledged her headline to the party.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: She reaches out a gloved hand and gives your sleeve a quick, neat tug to straighten the seam.
SAY: No need to get misty in the front row, darling, it spoils the powder.
SAY: Just keep your boots moving when the music starts, and I will handle the rest.
REASON: You thanked me for standing with the party to the end.
INSPIRE: Chose her friends over top billing.
